failures.title: Mercedes M264 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Cylinder Head Cracking and Coolant Loss
items.whatHappens: The M264 has developed a documented pattern of cylinder head cracking, particularly in the valve bridge area between the exhaust valves. This leads to internal coolant leaks, misfires, and white smoke from the exhaust. If ignored, coolant ingress can hydrolock the cylinders or wash away cylinder wall oil, leading to catastrophic bottom-end failure.
items.repairVsReplace: While a standalone cylinder head replacement is possible, the labour intensity and risk of underlying block damage often make a full Mercedes M264 engine replacement the more reliable long-term solution.

items.title: 48V ISG (Integrated Starter Generator) Contamination
items.whatHappens: In models equipped with the EQ Boost 48V mild-hybrid system, the ISG is mounted directly between the engine and transmission. Seal failures within the ISG can allow electrical coolant or oil to migrate into the engine bay or internal components, triggering warning lights and potential engine shutdowns.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught early, the ISG unit and associated seals can be replaced. However, if contamination has severely degraded the engine oil or caused internal scoring, a full rebuilt Mercedes M264 unit is required to prevent repeat failures.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the Mercedes M264
variants.intro: The M264 engine code is stamped directly onto the engine block, typically located on a machined pad near the oil filter housing or on the cylinder head. It is also clearly listed on your vehicle's V5C registration document under "Engine Number" and can be decoded from the full VIN via a Mercedes dealer or online checker. Common Confusion Warning: Owners frequently confuse the M264 with its predecessor, the M274, or the smaller M260. While they share a similar modular architecture, the M264 features a revised turbocharger setup, updated engine management software, and, in many applications, the integrated 48V ISG system. Fitting an M274 or M260 as a direct replacement will result in ECU incompatibility, wiring loom mismatches, and potential mounting issues.

relatives.description: - The M274 it replaced featured a similar modular architecture but lacked the integrated 48V mild-hybrid system and had different turbocharger mounting points.
- The smaller displacement predecessor found in A-Class and CLA models, which shares some architectural DNA but is not a direct swap for the M264.
The latest evolution of this modular family, featuring further electrification and updated thermal management to address earlier cooling vulnerabilities.
- The 1.3-litre variant of this modern modular family, suited for lighter compact models rather than the mid-size applications of the M264.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement Mercedes M264 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used Mercedes M264 is only advisable for lower-mileage host vehicles (e.g., newer A-Class or C-Class models) and *only* if accompanied by a full service history proving regular oil changes and no prior cylinder head or ISG-related repairs. Without this history, the risk of inheriting the same cracking or contamination issues is unacceptably high.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: This is the most recommended route for the M264. A proper reconditioned unit will include a brand-new or updated cylinder head, revised ISG seals (if applicable), and refreshed turbocharger components, directly addressing the engine's known weak points out of the box.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified if your original M264 suffered catastrophic coolant ingestion that scored the cylinder walls or damaged the crankshaft bearings. A specialist rebuild will machine the block, fit updated head components, and upgrade all cooling and lubrication pathways to prevent a repeat failure.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Sourcing a replacement is only half the job. Our network provides full supply and fit services, ensuring the engine is installed by Mercedes-specialist technicians with a nationwide warranty backing both the labour and the unit.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: For modern hosts like the W205 C-Class or X253 GLC, current UK market values typically sit between £12,000 and £25,000. With a reconditioned M264 replacement costing from £3,500 (plus fitting), the repair cost generally represents 20-40% of the vehicle's current market value, making replacement a financially viable option compared to older generations. However, always evaluate the specific condition and mileage of your vehicle before committing.

items.question: How much does a Mercedes M264 engine replacement cost in the UK?
items.answer: A Mercedes M264 engine replacement typically costs between £3,500 and £6,000 for a reconditioned supply-only unit . Fitted costs generally add £650-£910 for independent specialist labour, and fully rebuilt units with upgraded components can reach £5,000-£8,000 supply-only. Compare M264 engine replacement quotes from vetted UK specialists.

items.question: What is the most common failure with the Mercedes M264 engine?
items.answer: The most documented failure pattern for the M264 is cylinder head cracking, particularly in the valve bridge area, leading to internal coolant loss and misfires. Early warning signs include unexplained coolant drops and white exhaust smoke, and in 48V mild-hybrid models, Integrated Starter Generator (ISG) seal failures can also cause internal contamination. Get quotes for a rebuilt M264 with these known weaknesses addressed.

items.question: Which Mercedes models use the M264 engine?
items.answer: The M264 is fitted to core Mercedes-Benz models from 2017 onwards, including the C-Class (W205), E-Class (W213), GLC (X253), and A-Class (W177). It powers badges ranging from the C200 and C300 to the GLC300 and E350, and you should always verify your exact fitment via registration lookup, as some markets or late-build models may use the newer M254. Confirm your exact M264 fitment before requesting a quote.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned Mercedes M264 engine?
items.answer: A reconditioned Mercedes M264 is strongly recommended over a used unit due to the known cylinder head cracking and 48V ISG contamination risks. Used units carry a high risk of inheriting the same latent defects unless accompanied by stamped proof of preventative head replacement, whereas reconditioned units include updated cylinder heads and revised ISG seals, providing a reliable long-term solution. View our reconditioned Mercedes M264 engine options with 12-month warranties.

items.question: How do I know if my car has the M264 and not the M274 or M260?
items.answer: The M264 engine code is stamped on the engine block near the oil filter housing and is listed on your V5C registration document. It is commonly confused with the older M274 or the smaller M260, but these are not direct interchange replacements due to ECU and wiring loom differences, and fitting the wrong revision will result in compatibility errors and potential mounting issues. Enter your registration above to confirm your exact M264 engine code.
